Italian:
da, a partire da — from; from … onward
via, via da — away; off
giù — down (chiefly in military commands)
togliere — remove (in removal instructions)
The choice depends on the sense and context.

Preposition and adverb.

【General meanings】
① From; from ... onward, marking a starting point in time, space, quantity, etc.
② Away; off; leaving. As a stage direction: exit.
③ Detached; off, as of a button.
④ Down; lower, chiefly in military commands.

【Examples in musical contexts】
[GM]
German: Dämpfer allmählich ab
English: Gradually remove the mutes.

[RW: Oper]
German: Sie eilen ab.
English: They hurry off.

[RS: Oper]
German: die ganze Steigerung von hier ab durchaus parodistisch!
English: The whole build-up from here on is to be entirely parodic!

【Usage notes】
“Remove the mute” (Dämpfer ab, Sordinen ab, referring to an external mute; corresponding to senza sordino for string and wind instruments); “From the indicated bar or beat”; “Exit the stage.”

【References】
[Duden: ab (adverb)](https://www.duden.de/rechtschreibung/ab_Adverb) / [IDS: ab (preposition)](https://grammis.ids-mannheim.de/praepositionen/299302)

Italian:
smorzare, attutire

【General meanings】
① Reduce or soften the strength or effect of sound, vibration, impact, etc.
② Figuratively, subdue or temper the intensity of an emotion or similar response.

【Usage notes】
On percussion instruments, damping reduces or stops the after-ring by restraining the vibration of the head, metal plate or other vibrating part. On timpani, for example, the after-ring can be stopped by touching the head with the hand. The method and timing depend on the instrument, notation and musical context.

【References】
[Duden: abdämpfen](https://www.duden.de/rechtschreibung/abdaempfen) / [VSL: Timpani](https://www.vsl.co.at/academy/percussion/timpani) / [Treccani: smorzare](https://www.treccani.it/vocabolario/smorzare/)

Italian:
coordinato — coordinated
accordato — tuned
bilanciato — balanced (when referring to balance)
These expressions are similar in meaning; the choice depends on the sense and context.

Abgestimmte is an inflected adjectival form of abgestimmt, the past participle of abstimmen.

【General meanings】
Adjusted, coordinated or brought into agreement with one another or with a given standard; matched or coordinated when referring to clothing, for example.

【Examples in musical contexts】
“Tuned to the required pitches,” referring to bells or other instruments.

In the fifth movement of Mahler's SYMPHONIE III, abgestimmte Glocken refers to bells with the specified pitches.

【References】
[IDS: abstimmen](https://grammis.ids-mannheim.de/verbs/view/400251/2) / [Document held by the International Gustav Mahler Society](https://www.gustav-mahler.org/archiv/veranstaltungsprogramme/v-001/V-001-000002.pdf) / [Treccani: accordare](https://www.treccani.it/vocabolario/accordare/)

Reference score: [Mahler, SYMPHONIE III (Universal/Dover edition): printed p. 190 / PDF p. 194](https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/3/33/IMSLP71001-PMLP57638-Mahler_-_Symphony_No._3_%28orch._score%29.pdf#page=194)

Italian:
diminuire, calare — decrease; diminish
togliere, levare — take off; remove

【General meanings】
① Decrease, diminish or wane (in amount, degree, strength, etc.).
② Take off or remove (a hat, glasses, etc.).
③ Decrease in weight; lose body weight.
④ Pick up (the telephone receiver).

【Examples in musical contexts】
[GM]
German: nehmen nach und nach die Dämpfer ab
English: Gradually remove the mutes.

[RW: Oper]
German: Die beiden Fermaten müssen von besonders langer Dauer sein, um nach dem schnelleren Anschwellen ein sehr allmähliches Abnehmen ausführen zu lassen.
English: Both fermatas must be held for a particularly long time, to allow a very gradual diminuendo after the quicker crescendo.

[RS: Oper]
German: Sklavinnen bringen Salben und die sieben Schleier und nehmen Salome die Sandalen ab.
English: The female slaves bring perfumed ointments and the seven veils and remove Salome’s sandals.

【Usage notes】
In the context of a gradual reduction in volume, it corresponds to diminuendo or decrescendo. When used of tempo, it denotes a decrease in speed. Dämpfer abnehmen means “remove the mute(s).”

In GM, the term is used in both senses ① and ②.

【References】
[Duden: abnehmen](https://www.duden.de/rechtschreibung/abnehmen) / [Mahler Foundation: Terminology](https://mahlerfoundation.net/mahler/the-man/terminology/)

Italian:
strappare (via) — tear off; rip away
abbattere — demolish
interrompersi — break off; be interrupted (intransitive)
interrompere, troncare — interrupt; cut off (transitive)

【General meanings】
① Transitive: tear off or rip away; demolish (a building).
② Intransitive: break off abruptly, be interrupted, or cease (speech, contact, etc.).

【Examples in musical contexts】

English: Cut off the sound sharply.

[RS: Oper]
German: Er reisst sich das Kranzgewinde ab und wirft es auf den Tisch.
English: He tears the wreath from his head and throws it onto the table.

【Usage notes】
Applied to a note or phrase: “cut off abruptly”; to the musical flow: “break up.” Nicht abreißen means “do not cut off abruptly.”

[Duden: abreißen](https://www.duden.de/rechtschreibung/abreiszen) / [Mahler, SYMPHONIE III: Flute 2 part (PDF p. 15 / printed p. 15)](https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/e/ec/IMSLP960744-PMLP57638-Mahler_3_full_parts-17-31.pdf#page=15)

Italian:
respingere; (mus.) staccare, staccato

【General meanings】
① Push off or away, move something away with a push, or repel (physically).
② Arouse disgust or cause displeasure.
③ Sell off or dispose of (something unwanted).

【Examples in musical contexts】
“Play staccato”; “Detach and separate the notes”; “Play detached notes” (on string instruments).

On wind instruments, the notes may be separated by tonguing. The sharpness, length and force of the separation depend on the instrument, articulation marks, tempo, dynamics and surrounding directions.

Italian:
deviare da, scostarsi da — deviate or depart from

② Differ or diverge in form, character, opinion, etc.

Italian:
fare attenzione a, badare a — pay attention to; heed
rispettare, stimare — respect; esteem (according to construction and sense)

【General meanings】
① With auf followed by the accusative: pay attention to, take care with, or heed something.
② With a direct object: respect, esteem, or attach importance to someone or something.

【Examples in musical contexts】
[GM]
German: möglichst zahlreich, aber auf die dynamischen Zeichen sorgfältig achtend
English: With as many players as possible, but observing the dynamic markings carefully.

[RW: Oper]
German: mit der fürchterlichsten Anstrengung, um gehört zu werden, seinen Blick nur auf Lohengrin geheftet und der Andringenden nicht achtend.
English: With the most desperate effort to make himself heard, his gaze fixed solely on Lohengrin, ignoring those pressing in on him.

[RS: Oper]
German: ohne auf Waldner zu achten; nur zu Arabella
English: Ignoring Waldner; only to Arabella.

【Usage notes】
In music, it refers to attention to rhythm, dynamics or instructions. Where the context concerns listening to another part, it can be rendered as “listen carefully to the other parts.”

Italian:

Italian:
vista, scena, contemplazione
Masculine noun (der Anblick). The genitive singular is des Anblicks or des Anblickes, the nominative plural die Anblicke, and the dative plural den Anblicken. The sense of looking or contemplating has no plural. Anblicke in the corpus is an older dative singular.

【General meanings】
① A sight, view, or appearance presented to the eye.
② The act of looking at or contemplating something; bei jemandes Anblick means on seeing someone.

【Examples in musical contexts】
[RW: Oper]
German: Wotan erwacht, und erhebt sich ein wenig; sein Blick wird sogleich vom Anblick der Burg gefesselt.
English: Wotan awakens and raises himself a little; the sight of the castle immediately rivets his gaze.

Italian:
fermare, arrestare, trattenere

【General meanings】
① To stop (a person or vehicle); to bring to a halt; to call someone to a stop.
② To hold (one's breath).
③ To continue; to persist (of a state, the weather, etc.).
④ To train or urge (someone to do something).

【Examples in musical contexts】
[GM]
German: Anmerkung für den Dirigenten und Sänger : 𝄐 bedeutet hier nur ein kurzes Anhalten auf dem Taktstrich und nicht etwa eine Fermate. [Anmerkung Mahlers]
English: Note for the conductor and singer: Here the symbol 𝄐 indicates only a brief pause at the barline, not a fermata (Mahler’s note).

[RW: Oper]
German: Etwas anhalten.
English: With a slight pause.

[RS: Oper]
German: hält an, ganz in sein Bild versunken
English: He pauses in his singing, completely absorbed in the scene he has evoked.

【Usage notes】
“To hold back (the tempo)”; “to restrain (ritenuto)”; “to pause”; “to sustain (a note).”

In GM, anhalten is rendered as “slower”; in RW, as “with a pause,” among other translations. It can describe holding back or momentarily stopping something already in motion. In musical contexts, its nuance can be close to the Italian ritenuto (slower; restrained), firmly holding the tempo back at that moment.

Footnote example
The noun Anhalten is rendered here as “a pause.” A footnote to Mahler's Das himmlische Leben, a setting of a poem from Des Knaben Wunderhorn, reads “𝄐 bedeutet hier nur ein kurzes Anhalten auf dem Taktstrich und nicht etwa eine Fermate.” In the GM entry, this passage is translated as “Here the symbol 𝄐 indicates only a brief pause at the barline, not a fermata”.

Performance interpretation
This brief pause can also be understood as applying the brakes to the forward motion of the music and momentarily holding it back. One possible performance interpretation is restraint accompanied by an inner tension, like deliberately holding one's breath (Atem anhalten).

Gehalten can refer to sustaining tone and phrasing, in a sense close to tenuto or sostenuto, as well as to restraining the tempo or expression. Its distinction from anhalten depends on the particular use and the surrounding context. See also the entry for gehalten.

A combination of auf and ab.

【General meanings】
① Up and down; back and forth.
② As the noun das Auf und Ab: rises and falls, ups and downs, or fluctuations.

【Examples in musical contexts】
[GM]
German: Pater ecstaticus (auf und abschwebend)
English: Ecstatic Father (floating up and down).

[RW: Oper]
German: Er hält sich die Ohren zu und geht verzweiflungsvoll, sich mit sich beratend, die Gasse vor dem Fenster auf und ab.
English: He covers his ears and, in despair, walks up and down the lane in front of the window, deliberating with himself.

English: Likewise running up and down.

【Usage notes】
In bar 164 of the Andante of Mahler’s SYMPHONIE VI (listed as movement III in this resource), auf- und abwogend means “moving in rising and falling waves.” Wogen means to surge or move up and down in waves.
In Part II of SYMPHONIE VIII, at bar 219, Pater ecstaticus (auf und abschwebend) describes the character floating up and down. Schweben means to float, drift or remain suspended in the air.
In [RW: Oper] and [RS: Oper], the phrase is rendered as “back and forth” or “up and down,” according to the movement being described.

An abbreviation for the thematic catalogue of Richard Strauss's works compiled by Erich Hermann Müller von Asow (Asow-Verzeichnis), and for the catalogue numbers used in it.

The differences between TrV and AV, and why two catalogues exist: their purposes and roles

Some works by Richard Strauss (1864–1949) have opus numbers assigned during his lifetime, but many of his early and late works, studies, occasional pieces, songs, and other compositions have no opus number. Later scholars therefore compiled catalogues to organize and identify his complete output systematically. The principal examples are AV (Asow numbers) and TrV (Trenner numbers). The background to their coexistence, and their respective characteristics and roles, are as follows.

1. AV (Asow-Verzeichnis / Müller von Asow numbers)
Compiler: Erich Hermann Müller von Asow
Full title: Richard Strauss: Thematisches Verzeichnis (three volumes, issued in instalments between 1955 and 1974)
Characteristics and role: A substantial thematic catalogue (a catalogue giving the opening notes of musical themes), published after Richard Strauss's death, and a large-scale catalogue of his works.
It serves as a scholarly reference work and collection of source information, covering in great detail the thematic incipits of individual works, instrumentation, circumstances of composition, locations of autograph manuscripts, dates and performers of first performances, early printed editions, and other information. Müller von Asow died while compiling the third volume, which was supplemented and completed by Alfons Ott and Franz Trenner. The works are divided into categories, including those with and without opus numbers, and arranged chronologically within those categories. Besides works without opus numbers, the third volume includes lost works, arrangements, fragments, unrealized projects, and other material.

2. TrV (Trenner-Verzeichnis / Trenner numbers)
Compiler: Franz Trenner
Full title: Richard Strauss: Werkverzeichnis (published in 1985 / a 1993 version including thematic incipits, and a second revised edition in 1999, completed and continued by Florian Trenner)
Characteristics and role: Incorporating research and information about the works that followed the publication of Müller von Asow's catalogue, this catalogue reorganized the works as a whole in order of composition (chronological order). Its chronological arrangement (from the earliest studies of 1870 to the final works of 1949) is useful for tracing the development of Richard Strauss's creative activity and establishing and identifying dates of composition. The Richard-Strauss-Quellenverzeichnis (Richard Strauss Sources Catalogue / RSQV) takes TrV as its starting point and corrects and supplements the information about the works. TrV is also referenced in research and scholarly editions such as Richard Strauss Werke. Kritische Ausgabe (the critical edition of Richard Strauss's works), although information based on either catalogue may require correction in the light of subsequent research.

In summary:
AV: A comprehensive thematic catalogue (Thematisches Verzeichnis) for investigating thematic incipits, detailed historical and bibliographical information, and the circumstances in which works were composed.
TrV: A chronological catalogue of works (Chronologisches Werkverzeichnis) that orders and identifies the works as a whole chronologically on the basis of research available at the time of publication.

Thus, the catalogues differ in their origins and organization: an earlier, detailed thematic catalogue (AV), followed by a catalogue (TrV) that reorganized the works as a whole chronologically in light of subsequent research. However, AV also uses chronological ordering within its categories, and versions of TrV from 1993 onward also contain thematic incipits. They are consulted as complementary resources, and there are examples of both numbers appearing together in the official list of works.

Italian:
accompagnante

② Accompanying or occurring alongside another phenomenon, etc.

English: Doctor Marianus is only to sing in accompaniment, without standing out.

English: The preceding nine eighth notes are to be taken as three triplets over the first two beats of the measure, so that the vocal line, on the last note of the measure, falls exactly on the third beat each time. 【General meanings】
① Resolute, determined, firm, strong-willed.
② Prescribed, fixed, certain (specific), definite, clear, distinct.

【Examples in musical contexts】
[GM]
German: bestimmt
English: Resolutely.

[RW: Oper]
German: Es ist anzunehmen, dass ein einzelner Hornbläser nicht bestimmt genug hörbar wird,und es möge daher diese Stelle, je nach Befinden, noch durch eine Trompete verstärkt werden; jedenfalls muss aber der Klang des Hornes vorherrschend bleiben.

English: Very resolutely.

【Usage notes】
“Resolutely”; “with determination”; “distinctly”; “making the notes or rhythm stand out clearly (in a marcato-like sense, where indicated by the context)”; “forcefully (with conviction).”

When applied to string playing, “breit gestrichen” means something like “with broad bow strokes”. For breit alone, “with a sense of breadth” may also be suitable. “nicht breit” may also suggest keeping the tempo taut. It may, however, ask a particular part not to broaden its notes or rhythm too much, rather than require a change in the overall tempo.

【General meanings】

② A damper on enthusiasm; a letdown; something that takes the wind out of one's sails.
③ Regionally, a steamer for cooking.
【Musical meanings】
① A mute for a string or wind instrument (sordina), reducing volume and changing the tone colour.
② A piano damper (smorzatore), which stops a string's vibration by coming into contact with it.

【Usage notes】
For removable mutes, mit Dämpfer means “with the mute on” (con sordino), and Dämpfer ab / weg means “remove the mute” (senza sordino). See also “Dämpfer auf.”

【References】
[Duden: Dämpfer](https://www.duden.de/rechtschreibung/Daempfer) / [Langenscheidt: German–English Dämpfer](https://de.langenscheidt.com/deutsch-englisch/daempfer) / [Treccani: smorzatore](https://www.treccani.it/vocabolario/smorzatore/)

Remove the mute

Short for “Dämpfer abnehmen” or “Dämpfer absetzen.” See “Dämpfer auf.”

Put the mute on

In GM, Dämpfer auf is an instruction equivalent to Dämpfer aufsetzen (to put the mute on). By contrast, Dämpfer ab corresponds to Dämpfer abnehmen or Dämpfer absetzen and means 「remove the mute」.

Here, auf denotes the action of attaching the mute to the instrument. For example, on string instruments the mute is attached to the bridge, while on brass instruments it is fitted to the bell. Dämpfer auf／Dämpfer ab thus form a pair of instructions meaning 「put the mute on／take the mute off」.

On the other hand, auf can also generally mean 「open」. When offen (open) or gestopft (stopped) is indicated for brass instruments, its relationship to open tones, hand-stopping, the use of a mute, and so forth must be interpreted according to the instrument and the surrounding context. The auf in Dämpfer auf does not denote this sense of 「open」, but rather the fitting of the mute.

Italian:

【General meanings】
① (Of a manner) excessively humble, servile, submissive, subservient.
② (Archaic) devout, devoted.

【Examples in musical contexts】

German: sehr devot
English: Very deferentially.

【Usage notes】
“Obsequiously,” “humbly,” “as if rubbing one’s hands in ingratiation,” “submissively,” “(excessively) deferentially,” “bowing and scraping.”

It is rendered as “humbly,” among other possibilities.
Demütig: humble, reverent (neutral to mildly positive).
Devot: excessively submissive / servile / ingratiating (strongly negative in connotation).
In modern German, devot seems to have a strong sense of being servile and eager to please the other person.

This comparison describes a relative tendency in connotation: demütig can also express submissiveness or self-abasement. Sense ② of devot represents historical usage and should be distinguished from its modern general meaning. The examples “as if rubbing one’s hands in ingratiation” and “bowing and scraping” figuratively convey an excessively deferential manner; devot itself does not necessarily prescribe hand-rubbing or bowing.

【Usage notes】
In musical directions, durchaus and durchweg (also durchwegs) can overlap in the sense of “throughout” or “consistently”.
● durchaus:
Emphasizes degree or thoroughness, as in “absolutely” or “without fail”. It can reinforce determination, a state or a quality, and can also be rendered “throughout” in music.
● durchweg (or durchwegs):
Emphasizes consistency over time or space: “throughout” or “without exception”, with the same state maintained across the whole.

“Simply (semplice)”; “with simplicity”; “without ornamentation”; “plainly (without elaborate display)”; “without excessive emotion (when accompanied by directions to avoid sentimentality or exaggeration).”

Italian:
tenuto, sostenuto, trattenuto
Past participle of halten.

【General meanings】
① Kept, held, maintained.
② Sustained, prolonged (of a sound or a duration).
③ Calm, reserved, restrained, measured.

【Examples in musical contexts】
[GM]
German: Gehaltener
English: With the tempo held back more.

[RW: Oper]
German: Sehr gemessen, vornehm, huldvoll gehalten.
English: Maintaining a very measured, refined and gracious manner.

[RS: Oper]
German: Zimmer des Sir Morosus, Weiter, unordentlich gehaltener Raum mit vielen Zeichen, die erkennen lassen, daß hier ein ehemaliger Seemann haust: Schiffsmodelle, Fahnen, Gewehre, Anker, Fischgerippe, Takelwerk. Besonders auffällig, daß alle Türen mit dichten Vorhängen oder Säcken geschützt sind.
English: Sir Morosus's room. A spacious, untidy room with many signs that a former sailor lives here: model ships, flags, guns, anchors, fish skeletons and rigging. Especially striking is the fact that all the doors are protected by thick curtains or sacks.

【Usage notes】
“With the notes sustained (sostenuto)”; “sustained (tenuto)”; “restrained”; “with a restrained tone.”

GM generally renders it as “with the tempo held back,” but the translation needs to vary according to context, using expressions such as “with the notes sustained” (≒ sostenuto) or “with a restrained flow.” It may refer to sustaining the tone fully and maintaining the flow of a phrase, or to keeping the tempo or expression calm and restraining the overall flow. These meanings may overlap; where the emphasis lies depends on the placement of the marking and the surrounding context. Sustaining tone and phrasing is close to the Italian sostenuto (“supported”) or tenuto (“held”), but is not a blanket instruction to lengthen every note beyond its written value.
The comparative form gehaltener also conveys the sense of “more” or “even more.”

By contrast, “anhalten” means “to hold back (something that is in motion), to bring it to a stop, or to apply the brakes”; in music, depending on the context, it is probably close to the Italian ritenuto (“immediately slower, held back”), which suggests holding the tempo back at that point.
See also the entry “anhalten.”

Italian:
periodo cantabile, periodo melodico
A compound noun formed from Gesang (“song”) + s (a linking element) + Periode (“period,” “span”).

【Examples in musical contexts】
“A cantabile period”; “a lyrical thematic section”; “the second theme group (especially in Bruckner's symphonies).”

This is a characteristic term used by Anton Bruckner for the “second theme group” in the sonata-form movements of his symphonies. It was not coined by Bruckner; rather, he is understood to have given substance, in keeping with his own sense of form, to a term derived from the compositional theory associated with Johann Christian Lobe. In German-language terminology, the first thematic area is called Hauptsatz or Hauptthema, and the second Seitensatz (secondary section) or Seitenthema (secondary theme). The closing area (often a third theme group in Bruckner) is called Schlusssatz (closing section) or Schlussthema (closing theme / third theme). In Bruckner, the second theme group is called Gesangsperiode (lyrical thematic section / singing period). Its character can be described as follows.

【Contrasts of character】

In Bruckner's sonata forms, the first theme (Hauptsatz) often has a “rhythmic, motivic, grand” character, contrasted with a second theme (Gesangsperiode) that is “melodic, lyrical (cantabile), and contrapuntal.” The following third theme (Schlusssatz) can display qualities such as “rhythmic energy, a powerful orchestral tutti, or a chorale-like character,” although these do not invariably occur together. This contrast suggests that the second theme is more than a merely subsidiary theme: it can be understood as a distinct, songful region (Periode).

【Structural independence】

Bruckner's “second theme” often forms an extended section (group), with several interwoven parts, rather than simply a single melody. It is therefore reasonable to describe it as a Periode (a section / a span) rather than only a Thema (theme).

The term is particularly characteristic of Bruckner and Bruckner scholarship when used for the second theme group in sonata form, but its background lies in nineteenth-century theories of form, including Lobe's.

barrato — crossed out; deleted
Past participle of the verb streichen (to stroke, rub, or cross out).

【General meanings】
① Stroked or rubbed.
② Applied (of paint, etc.).
③ Crossed out or deleted (of letters, text, etc.).

【Examples in musical contexts】
“Sustained (with a long bow stroke)”; “drawn out (with a long bow stroke)”; “using a full bow (in Bruckner)”; “played with the bow”; “deleted”.

The word can also refer to octave notation. The prime sign (′) placed to the upper right of a note name is called a Strich (stroke); the number of these strokes indicates which octave the note belongs to. For example, dreimal gestrichenes C means “three-line C”.

【Use of gestrichen in Bruckner】
The word is used to call for ample bowing and a clear profile for individual notes. Besides a return to ordinary bowing, it may concern fullness of tone or a separate bow stroke for each note. Changing bow direction for each note does not necessarily mean leaving a silence between notes.

【Use of gezogen in Bruckner】
The word suggests using ample bow and sustaining a full tone. The German verb ziehen (to draw or pull) has connotations of drawing a line and extending something at length. Oeser discusses lang gezogen, gezogen, gestrichen, and kurz gestrichen as differentiated directions within the practice of bowing each note separately. In his account, fullness of tone and a clear melodic profile go together.

When considering Bruckner’s sound, the metaphor “organ-like” may offer a useful image for sustaining a full tone. The actual bow speed and pressure are adjusted according to the dynamics, register, phrasing, and other circumstances.

In SYMPHONIE V, movement I, the cellos and double basses are marked “gestrichen, mehr gezogen” at bar 174 and “gestrichen, gezogen” at bar 176, with both words combined in the same direction.

【Use of gestrichen in GM】
After special techniques such as pizz. or col legno, gestrichen (or wieder gestrichen) can indicate a return to ordinary bowing. There are also examples such as breit gestrichen, kurz gestrichen, and lang gestrichen that describe the breadth or length of the bow stroke. For example, breit gestrichen is translated here as “With broad bow strokes.” and kurz gestrichen as “With short bow strokes.”

【Use of gezogen in GM】
The collected examples include breit gezogen, lang gezogen, and lang gezogen (viel Bogen). The adopted translations are “Play with long (ample) bow strokes.” for lang gezogen and “Play with long (ample) bow strokes (using plenty of bow).” for lang gezogen (viel Bogen).

It is best not to read Bruckner’s directions concerning bowing or sonority simply as a return to arco. Thinking of GM’s return instructions as “How to play” and Bruckner’s directions concerning fullness of tone as “How it sounds” may help bring out the differences between these contexts. Playing technique and sound are, however, connected in both composers.

Italian:
maggiordomo, intendente

【General meanings】
(In older usage) A steward, butler, or household administrator who manages the domestic affairs of a large residence or court and supervises its servants.

The following is a guide to servants, attendants, and domestic workers in RS’s Der Rosenkavalier Op.59. Even the same terms—Diener, Lakai, and Livree—can have substantially different functions depending on whose household they belong to. It is therefore useful to distinguish the Marschallin’s household, Faninal’s household, Baron Ochs’s entourage, and the inn staff. Octavian’s own attendants, who appear in Act II, must also be distinguished. Since differentiating every term in translation would become extremely cumbersome, some are grouped together on the search page.

【Qualification concerning rank】
The ranks given below and the hierarchy at the end are provisional classifications from the original draft; they have not been verified as a uniform historical hierarchy of posts. Duties, relationships with the employer, household affiliation, and assessments of characters on stage must be distinguished. In particular, the same Leopold is called Kammerdiener, junger Kammerlakai, Leibkammerdiener, Leiblakai, Lakai, and other names in this work. Differences in terminology therefore cannot simply be taken to indicate separate characters or differences in social rank.

●Almosenier
A post responsible for administering alms, or a disreputable former cleric. Originally, this was the title of a cleric responsible for charitable work at a court or in the residence of a great noble. When Baron Ochs uses this word, its archaic, grandiose sound itself comically conveys his character as an anachronistic provincial nobleman.
【Rendering used】Almoner
【Rank: low】One of Baron Ochs’s personal followers. Despite his pompous title, he is in fact a dubious former cleric whose social standing is incomparably lower than that of the regular servants in the Marschallin’s household.

●Bediente
“Household servant,” with a somewhat official, impersonal tone. More formal than Diener, it strongly suggests a member of the “staff” employed by a household or master. The emphasis is on the staff as a group rather than on individual personalities.
【Renderings used】Household servant, household servants
【Rank: middle to lower】A general term for male servants. It refers primarily to ordinary workers who support the running of the residence, rather than to senior posts such as steward or valet. It is approximately equivalent in rank to Diener (servant), but Bediente has a somewhat more institutional or organizational tone.

●Diener
The broadest and most basic term for “one who serves.” It is not restricted to any particular duty, but focuses on the act of serving a master. It conveys a sense of personal service by a servant.
【Renderings used】Servant, servants
【Rank: middle to lower】The basic rank of male servants: an ordinary servant without a special job title. It is approximately equivalent in rank to Bediente (household servant), but Diener more strongly suggests an individual serving another person. In Der Rosenkavalier Op.59, however, an unqualified Diener does not always refer to the same household affiliation: depending on the context, he may belong to the Marschallin’s household, Faninal’s household, or Baron Ochs’s entourage.

●Dienerschaft
The entire body or organization of servants. A collective noun referring to an organized staff headed by a steward. The standing of a residence is reflected in the quality and size of its Dienerschaft.
【Renderings originally preferred】Servants; depending on the context, “attendants” or “the household staff”
【Rank: the entire structure】The basic rendering is “servants,” in keeping with Diener. Depending on the scene, however, it may be translated flexibly as “the household staff” or “attendants.” When used of Baron Ochs’s entourage, it often refers to his uncouth followers rather than to a refined household organization.

●Duenna
A supervisor or guardian of a young noblewoman. A specialized post originating in the Spanish court, often functioning as a nagging, conservative supervisor of female attendants.
【Rendering originally preferred】Chaperone
【Designation used】Duenna (Marianne)
【Rank: upper-middle】Sophie’s personal chaperone. She ranks above ordinary maids and has authority to supervise the young lady’s conduct, manners, and formal interactions. In Der Rosenkavalier Op.59, Jungfer Marianne Leitmetzerin can be treated as the character who performs this function.

●Faninals Bediente / Diener / Livree / Lakaien
Collective designations for the household servants, servants, footmen, and liveried footmen serving Faninal’s household. The libretto varies its terminology according to the scene, using such expressions as Faninalsche Bediente, Faninalsche Diener, Faninalsche Livree, and Faninalsche Lakaien. All can be classified as the body of servants belonging to Faninal’s residence.
【Renderings originally preferred】
Bediente: household servants
Diener: servants
Livree: liveried footmen
Lakaien: footmen
【Rendering used】Servants of the Faninal household
【Rank: middle to lower / household organization】In Act II, during the ceremonial presentation of the rose, they open and close doors, arrange chairs, serve wine and sweets, and receive visitors, visually expressing the standing of the household established by the upstart nobleman Faninal. At the same time, they become caught up in the uncouth behavior of Baron Ochs’s attendants, highlighting the breakdown of order within the house. In Act III, they assist Faninal and Sophie, who have hurried to the inn, and tend to Faninal when he is on the verge of fainting. They thus function as a group that sustains the stage portrayal of both the Faninal household’s dignity and its confusion. Although there are fine distinctions in meaning, it should be acceptable to group them under “servants of the Faninal household.”
【Note】Haushofmeister bei Faninal (the steward of Faninal’s household) is best considered separately as the managerial official who supervises this group.

●Hausknecht
A menial worker employed at an inn, a merchant’s establishment, or similar premises. Responsible for physical labor and of the lowest rank. He belongs to a different category from the servants in an aristocratic residence.
【Rendering used】Inn servant
【Rank: lowest / inn staff】A coarse menial worker employed behind the scenes at the inn. He appears in Act III and reinforces the inn’s practical, everyday atmosphere. He belongs to a different system from the hierarchy of servants in an aristocratic residence.

●Haushofmeister
A steward or head butler who oversees an entire residence belonging to a great noble or wealthy household. He heads the organization of servants and supervises ceremonial arrangements, finances, household operations, and the reception of visitors.
【Rendering originally preferred】Head butler
【Rendering used】Steward
【Rank: highest managerial post】The highest rank in the hierarchy of male servants in a residence. An important official who directs the Diener, Lakai, Bediente, and others and embodies the household’s standing. Both the steward of the Marschallin’s household and the steward of Faninal’s household make their employers’ social status visible on stage.

●Kammerdiener
A personal attendant serving in his master’s private rooms. Responsible for dressing him, looking after his personal belongings, and carrying out private errands; his master’s trust is essential.
【Rendering used】Valet
【Rank: high】A specialized post ranking above ordinary footmen. He is experienced and holds a high position because of his loyalty to his master and his permission to enter the master’s private space. Baron Ochs’s Kammerdiener, however, is portrayed as an uncouth, slovenly attendant, in contrast to the refinement originally associated with this title.

●Kammerlakai
A lower-ranking footman attached to the private rooms. He assists the valet and performs miscellaneous duties around the private apartments.
【Rendering originally preferred】Chamber footman
【Rank: middle】Below a Kammerdiener, but more closely connected to the private rooms than an ordinary Lakai. In Der Rosenkavalier Op.59, the term sometimes appears as a designation for Baron Ochs’s young close attendant Leopold and overlaps functionally with Leiblakai. For practical classification, it is therefore useful to group it with Leiblakai / junger Kammerlakai / Lakai des Barons.

●Kellner
A waiter employed at a commercial establishment, particularly an inn or restaurant. Not a servant in an aristocratic residence.
【Rendering used】Waiters
【Rank: external】Employees outside the hierarchical structure of aristocratic society. In the inn scene in Act III, they attend to the table, lighting, food, wine, and entrances and exits, arranging Baron Ochs’s secret rendezvous with Mariandel as an ordinary meal. Near the end, they join the Wirt (innkeeper), Musikanten (musicians), Hausknecht (inn servant), and others in crowding around the Baron to demand payment of bills and service charges, reducing aristocratic dignity to the obligation to pay in a commercial setting.

●kleiner Neger
A Black boy attendant responsible for carrying the train of a garment and performing duties like those of a personal servant. A decorative presence used to display status. The term is now discriminatory and requires care.
【Rendering used】Black boy
【Rank: special (lower)】His role is to carry the Marschallin’s train. Although a type of footman, he is less part of the ordinary hierarchy of servants than a decorative presence employed for aristocratic display, exoticism, and the demonstration of status.

●Lakaien / Bediente der Feldmarschallin
The group of footmen serving in the Marschallin’s residence. In Act I, they try to prevent Baron Ochs from forcing his way in and guard the boundary between the bedroom and the antechamber. During the morning reception, they also open and close doors, move furniture, organize visitors, and coordinate the movements of the Friseur, Sänger, and others.
【Renderings originally preferred】
Lakaien: footmen
Bediente: household servants
【Rendering used】Marschallin’s footmen
【Rank: middle to lower / servants in a great aristocratic residence】They belong to a separate organization from servants of the Faninal household and Baron Ochs’s attendants. They show that the Marschallin’s residence, although the setting is her private bedroom, is also a highly organized aristocratic space.

●Lakai
A lower-ranking footman in a residence. Responsible for miscellaneous duties such as opening and closing doors, showing visitors in, and running errands; he is often also stationed for ceremonial purposes or visual effect.
【Rendering used】Footman
【Rank: lower】Equivalent to, or slightly below, Bediente and Diener. He ranks considerably below a valet. He wears livery to display his master’s household standing but has no personal authority or managerial position. In Der Rosenkavalier Op.59, he may belong to the Marschallin’s household, Faninal’s household, or Baron Ochs’s entourage. It is therefore clearer to include his affiliation in the translation rather than simply calling him a “footman.”

●Leibjäger
A huntsman and bodyguard attached exclusively to his master. A rugged figure accompanying a provincial nobleman.
【Rendering used】Bodyguard-huntsman
【Rank: special (low)】Rather than a regular household servant, he is one of the personal followers whom Baron Ochs has brought from the countryside. He is portrayed as embodying ruggedness, intimidation, and the coarseness of the provincial nobility rather than manners or refinement.

●Leibkammerdiener
A personal valet who serves his master in close attendance. Responsible for the most confidential duties in the private rooms.
【Rendering used】Personal valet
【Rank: very high】Even closer to his master than a Kammerdiener, and equivalent to the highest rank among footmen. In Baron Ochs’s case, however, he may be portrayed as an uncouth member of the Baron’s personal entourage rather than as a senior valet possessing formal courtly refinement.

●Leiblakai
A footman in his master’s personal service. Not as high-ranking as a Kammerdiener, but close to his master.
【Rendering used】Personal footman
【Rank: special (low)】He has a special relationship with his master but is of low social standing. In Baron Ochs’s case, he is implied to be an illegitimate son and is portrayed as poorly trained and unrefined. Formally, he is a footman serving as a close attendant; in practice, he is an uncouth follower of a provincial nobleman.

●Leiblakai / junger Kammerlakai / Lakai des Barons
The young personal attendant closest to Baron Ochs. In the libretto, he can be classified as the character functioning as Leiblakai, junger Kammerlakai, and, in some scenes, Lakai des Barons.
【Renderings originally preferred】
Leiblakai: personal footman
junger Kammerlakai: young chamber footman
Lakai des Barons: the Baron’s footman
【Rendering used】Personal footman
【Rank: special (low)】He carries the case for the silver rose, accompanies the Baron to his secret rendezvous at the inn, and tries to clear a path for the Baron’s departure near the end. He is also implied to be the Baron’s illegitimate son and visually conveys the private, disorderly domestic arrangements of the Lerchenau household.

●Leute / Livree / Diener / Dienerschaft des Barons
Collective designations for the personal followers and body of liveried footmen whom Baron Ochs has brought from the countryside. Leute emphasizes their function as “the Baron’s people or followers”; Livree emphasizes their appearance and display of status as “a body of footmen in livery”; Diener / Dienerschaft emphasizes the organization of servants attending the Baron.
【Renderings originally preferred】
Leute des Barons: Baron Ochs’s followers
Livree des Barons: Baron Ochs’s body of liveried footmen
Diener des Barons: Baron Ochs’s servants
Dienerschaft des Barons: Baron Ochs’s organization of servants
【Rendering used】Baron Ochs’s attendants
【Rank: low / uncouth】They include the Almosenier, Kammerdiener / Leibkammerdiener, Leibjäger, Leopold / Leiblakai, and others. In contrast to the refined servant organizations of Vienna, they are portrayed as slovenly and uncouth in their behavior. In Act II, they behave in an intimidating and violent manner toward Sophie and servants of the Faninal household, collectively amplifying Baron Ochs’s vulgar character. In Act III, they again try to preserve the Baron’s dignity, but become caught up with the inn staff and the unfolding trap, visually heightening the collapse of his authority.

●Livree
Livery, or the body of footmen wearing it. A term symbolizing the authority of a household.
【Renderings originally preferred】Livery, liveried footmen
【Rank: symbolic】The quality of the tailoring symbolizes the household’s standing. When the term appears on its own, it may be translated as “livery” or “liveried footmen.” For Baron Ochs’s entourage, however, it is easier to classify it together with Leute / Livree / Diener / Dienerschaft des Barons (Baron Ochs’s attendants), and for Faninal’s household, with Faninals Bediente / Diener / Livree / Lakaien (servants of the Faninal household).

●Lümmel
An uncouth young man or lout. An insult, not a particular job title.
【Rendering used】Lout
【Rank: lowest stratum / outside the hierarchy】Not a formal rank among servants. The word indicates the coarseness, lack of manners, and violence of Baron Ochs’s followers and should be treated as an assessment of character or an insult rather than as a social rank.

●Magd
An ordinary female servant. Responsible for domestic work such as cleaning, laundry, and kitchen duties.
【Renderings used】Maid, maids
【Rank: lower】The basic rank of female servants. Below a Zofe. In Act II, the maids are chased by Baron Ochs’s attendants, revealing the coarseness of his party and the breakdown of order in Faninal’s residence.

●Zofe
A lady’s maid who attends to the personal needs of a noblewoman. A highly trusted figure.
【Rendering used】Lady’s maid
【Rank: high (among female servants)】Considerably higher-ranking than an ordinary maid. She is close to her mistress’s private life and may become a confidante. In Rosenkavalier, however, this is the designation used when Octavian disguises himself as Mariandel.

【Classification by rank: for reference only】
The following is not a verified hierarchy. In particular, note that alternative designations for the same person are sometimes placed at different levels.

【Highest managerial post】
Haushofmeister (steward / more specifically, head butler)

【Very high (attached exclusively to the master personally)】
Leibkammerdiener (personal valet)

【High (senior servants with access to the private rooms)】
Kammerdiener (valet)
Zofe (lady’s maid)

【Upper-middle (supervisory role)】
Duenna (chaperone / more specifically, guardian)

【Middle (lower-ranking posts connected with the private rooms)】
Kammerlakai (chamber footman)

【Middle to lower (ordinary male servants)】
Bediente (household servant)
Diener (servant)
Lakai (footman)
Lakaien / Bediente der Feldmarschallin (Marschallin’s footmen / more specifically, “footmen,” “household servants”)
Faninals Bediente / Diener / Livree / Lakaien (servants of the Faninal household / more specifically, “household servants,” “servants,” “liveried footmen,” “footmen”)

【Lower (ordinary female servants)】
Magd (maid, maids)

【Lower (followers of provincial nobles and similar attendants)】
Almosenier (almoner)
Leute / Livree / Diener / Dienerschaft des Barons (Baron Ochs’s attendants / more specifically, “followers,” “body of liveried footmen,” “servants,” “organization of servants”)

【Special (outside the residence, or with a particular background)】
Leiblakai / junger Kammerlakai / Lakai des Barons (personal footman / more specifically, “personal footman,” “young chamber footman,” “the Baron’s footman”)
Leibjäger (bodyguard-huntsman)
kleiner Neger (Black boy)

【External (not servants in an aristocratic residence)】
Kellner (waiters)

【Lowest stratum / outside the hierarchy】
Hausknecht (inn servant)
Lümmel (lout)

② Fervent, hot-tempered, or passionate in temperament or emotion.
③ Severe, as of an illness.

A number assigned by the Swiss musicologist Willy Hess in his Verzeichnis der nicht in der Gesamtausgabe veröffentlichten Werke Ludwig van Beethovens, published in 1957.

The Hess catalogue was not compiled simply to classify works without opus numbers. It catalogues works and materials omitted from the old Beethoven complete edition published by Breitkopf & Härtel in the nineteenth century. It therefore includes not only independent, completed works but also first versions, alternative versions, arrangements and reworkings, unfinished works, fragments, sketches, and composition exercises. Hess numbers can also be assigned to alternative versions or arrangements of works that have opus or WoO numbers, so the Hess, Op., and WoO systems are not mutually exclusive.

However, not all of the vast quantity of sketches left by Ludwig van Beethoven have Hess numbers. The Hess catalogue was compiled to gather works and materials for a supplement to the old Beethoven complete edition. It is therefore not a comprehensive catalogue of Beethoven’s sketches.

Whereas WoO numbers are used to classify works without opus numbers, Hess numbers are supplementary catalogue numbers for works and creative materials omitted from the old complete edition. The two catalogues have different inclusion criteria, and neither simply contains the other. The Hess catalogue includes completed works as well as alternative versions, arrangements and reworkings, unfinished works, fragments, sketches, and composition exercises; WoO also includes unfinished works.

In 2014, a revised catalogue, Ludwig van Beethoven: Thematisch-bibliographisches Werkverzeichnis, by Kurt Dorfmüller, Norbert Gertsch, Julia Ronge, and collaborators, was published. It retains the established Op. and WoO numbers and assigns Unv (Unvollendete Werke) 1–23 to a selection of unfinished works not included in the previous catalogue. Hess numbers are not its principal classification numbers, but they are given alongside the relevant entries or sources, and a concordance is provided.

Hess numbers may thus be understood as historical supplementary numbers assigned by Willy Hess to identify completed works, alternative versions, arrangements and reworkings, unfinished works, fragments, sketches, composition exercises, and similar materials omitted from the old Beethoven complete edition. They continue to be used to cross-reference older literature, scores, recordings, and research.

See also “WoO”.

An abbreviation for the catalogue of Joseph Haydn's works (Hoboken-Verzeichnis) compiled by the Dutch musicologist Anthony van Hoboken. Works are classified by genre and identified by a Roman-numeral group number followed by a number within that group. For example, Symphony No. 100 in G major is Hob. I:100. An overview of groups I–XXXI is given below; subsidiary categories such as Ia are omitted. There is also a group XXXII for pasticcios (works assembled from pre-existing pieces).

Hob. I: Symphonies (Symphonien)
Hob. II: Divertimenti in four or more parts (Divertimenti in 4 und mehr Stimmen)
Hob. III: String quartets (Streichquartette)
Hob. IV: Divertimenti in three parts (Divertimenti in 3 Stimmen)
Hob. V: String trios (Streichtrios)
Hob. VI: Various duos (Verschiedene Duos)
Hob. VII: Concertos for various instruments (Konzerte für verschiedene Instrumente)
Hob. VIII: Marches (Märsche)
Hob. IX: Dances (Tänze)
Hob. X: Various ensembles or divertimenti involving baryton (Werke mit Baryton / Divertimenti mit Baryton)
Hob. XI: Baryton trios (Barytontrios)
Hob. XII: Duos involving baryton, including those with a bass part (Duos mit Baryton, mit und ohne Bass)
Hob. XIII: Baryton concertos (Barytonkonzerte)
Hob. XIV: Divertimenti with piano (Divertimenti mit Klavier)
Hob. XV: Trios for violin (or flute), cello, and piano (Trios für Klavier, Violine (oder Flöte) und Violoncello)
Hob. XVI: Piano sonatas (Klaviersonaten)
Hob. XVII: Short piano pieces (Klavierstücke)
Hob. XVIII: Keyboard concertos (Klavierkonzerte)
Hob. XIX: Pieces for mechanical musical clocks (Stücke für Spieluhren)
Hob. XX: The Seven Last Words of Our Saviour on the Cross (Die sieben letzten Worte unseres Erlösers am Kreuze)
Hob. XXI: Oratorios (Oratorien)
Hob. XXII: Masses (Messen)
Hob. XXIII: Other sacred works (Kirchenwerke)
Hob. XXIV: Cantatas, choruses, and arias with orchestral accompaniment (Kantaten, Chöre und Arien mit Orchester)
Hob. XXV: Songs for several voices, including duets, trios, and quartets (Mehrstimmige Gesänge)
Hob. XXVI: Songs with piano accompaniment, and cantatas and choruses accompanied by a single instrument (Lieder mit Klavierbegleitung; Kantaten und Chöre mit Begleitung eines Instruments)
Hob. XXVII: Canons (Kanons)
Hob. XXVIII: Operas (Opern)
Hob. XXIX: Marionette operas and Singspiele (Marionetten-Opern und Singspiele)
Hob. XXX: Incidental music (Schauspielmusiken)
Hob. XXXI: Arrangements of Scottish and Welsh folk songs, and other arrangements (Bearbeitungen schottischer und walisischer Volkslieder und andere Bearbeitungen)

Feminine noun (die Höhle). The genitive singular is der Höhle, the nominative plural die Höhlen, and the dative plural den Höhlen. Höle in the corpus is an older spelling.

【General meanings】
① A cave or large hollow space, especially in rock or underground.
② An animal's underground den or burrow.
③ Disparagingly, a dark, damp, poor dwelling.
④ Colloquially, one's own familiar and sheltered room or retreat.

【Examples in musical contexts】
[RW: Oper]
German: Siegfried tritt in die Höle herein.
English: Siegfried comes into the cave.

[RS: Oper]
German: Ariadne tritt an den Eingang ihrer Höhle zurück
English: Ariadne withdraws to the entrance of her cave.

Italian:

Neuter noun (das Holz). Genitive singular des Holzes; normally uncountable as a material. Wood types or pieces have plural Hölzer, dative plural Hölzern. Bowling pins can take plural Holz.

【General meanings】
① Wood as a material, timber, or firewood.
② A type or piece of wood, a wooden rod or component, or a bowling pin.
③ Regionally or historically, a wood or forest.

【Examples in musical contexts】
[GM]
German: So stark anreißen, daß die Saiten an das Holz anschlagen.
English: Pluck so forcefully that the strings strike the fingerboard.

[RW: Oper]
German: Das englische Horn soll hier die Wirkung eines sehr kräftigen Naturinstrumentes, (wie das Alpenhorn), hervorbringen; es ist daher zu raten, je nach Befund des akustischen Verhältnisses, es durch Hoboen und Klarinetten zu verstärken, falls man nicht, was das Zweckmäßigste wäre, ein besonderes Instrument (aus Holz), nach dem Modell der Schweizer Alpenhörner, hierfür anfertigen lassen wollte, welches seiner Einfachheit wegen (da es nur die Naturskala zu haben braucht) weder schwierig noch kostbar sein wird.
English: The English horn should here produce the effect of a very powerful natural instrument (such as the alphorn). It is therefore advisable, according to the acoustic conditions, to reinforce it with oboes and clarinets, unless one chooses to have a special instrument (made of wood) constructed for this purpose on the model of the Swiss alphorns, which would be the most appropriate solution. Owing to its simplicity (as it need only have the natural harmonic series), such an instrument will be neither difficult nor expensive to make.

[RS: Oper]
German: Die Buben stürzen sich mit Geschrei aufs Haus und reissen, was an Holz nicht niet und nagelfest ist, herunter
English: The boys rush at the house with shouts and tear down all the wood that is not firmly fixed in place.

(Verified location in the reference score: Hindemith, Konzertmusik für Klavier, Blechbläser, und Harfen Op.49: movement I: bottom footnote; Klavierauszug also staff label)
(Reference score, Schott edition: PDF p. 3.)

A Black pageboy.

“Neger” was formerly used in Europe to refer to Black people, but is now regarded as a discriminatory term. When it appears in historical librettos or scores, it needs to be understood as an expression reflecting the society and racial attitudes of its time.

A related musical work is Claude Debussy’s Golliwogg’s Cake-walk. It is the sixth piece in the suite Children’s Corner, and the Golliwogg in its title refers to a rag doll caricaturing a Black person. The figure became widely known through a picture book published in 1895 and illustrated by Florence Kate Upton, and was also popular as a children’s toy. Its features, including its black face, large eyes and exaggerated lips, are connected with the imagery of contemporary minstrel shows, in which performers blackened their faces to portray Black people, and embody racial stereotypes.

The cakewalk is a dance that developed among enslaved Black people in America. One aspect of it involved imitating and satirizing the affected gestures and dances of the white upper classes. Its name derives from the practice of awarding a cake to the winner of a dance competition. It later spread through Europe and America as a form of stage entertainment and was also incorporated into Debussy’s music. In Golliwogg’s Cake-walk, both the dance and the doll bring together the reception of Black culture and representations of Black people at the time.

Debussy also composed a separate short piano piece using cakewalk rhythms, Le petit nègre (the little Black person).

【General meanings】
① A beater or mallet (for percussion instruments); a clapper (inside a bell).

In the Glockenspiel part in the first movement of Mahler's SYMPHONIE VII, the instruction "mit Klöppeln" appears and is translated there as “with mallets”. From a modern perspective, however, playing the Glockenspiel “with mallets” is a matter of course. Yet the “keyboard glockenspiel (Tastenglockenspiel)” was also in use in GM's time, and it is highly likely that SYMPHONIE VII likewise presupposes a keyboard glockenspiel (for example, the aria No.20 in Mozart's “The Magic Flute” (Bärenreiter p.258) bears the designation "Strumento d'acciaio (Glockenspiel)" (“instrument of steel”) and contains many multiple-note combinations and rapid passages, making it highly likely that a keyboard glockenspiel was intended). In that light, an instruction to play with “mallets” rather than a “keyboard” makes sense.

Lady Macbeth. O, eile! Eile her! damit ich meinen Geist in deinen giesse, durch meine tapfere Zunge diese Zweifel und Furchtgespenster aus dem Felde schlage, die dich wegschrecken von dem goldnen Reif, womit das Glück dich gern bekrönen möchte.

The German heading comes from Schiller’s adaptation (Act 1, Scene 9). The corresponding original passage in Shakespeare’s Macbeth, Act 1, Scene 5, reads as follows.

Lady Macbeth:
Hie thee hither,
That I may pour my spirits in thine ear,
And chastise with the valour of my tongue
All that impedes thee from the golden round,
Which fate and metaphysical aid doth seem
To have thee crown’d withal.

【Translation of the German quotation】
O, hurry! Come quickly!
Then I could pour my resolve into you,
and with the force of these courageous words
drive away all the doubts and spectres of fear
that keep you from the golden crown (kingship).
For fortune (fate) would gladly crown you with that crown.

The scene can be interpreted as follows. Having read Macbeth’s letter describing the witches’ prophecy, Lady Macbeth sees that her husband is “too kind to resolve to become king”. She decides to take on the task of pouring that resolve into him and driving out his hesitation through words. Here, “Geist” (“spirit”) means courage, boldness, and the ability to make ruthless decisions, while “tapfere Zunge” (“valiant tongue”) shows her awareness of the power of manipulative language as a weapon. “Goldner Reif” (“golden circlet”) is an indirect expression for the crown, while “Glück” (“fortune” or “luck”) can also be read as a perilous turn of phrase that presents the temptation to sin as though it were fate’s blessing.

(Reference score: printed p. 280 / PDF p. 10.)

Italian:

【General meanings】
① Having pith or marrow; substantial or full of substance.

【Examples in musical contexts】
“robusto”, “vigoroso”, “forcefully”, “robustly”, “with a full-bodied sound”.

In GM it is rendered with expressions such as “with weight” and “forcefully”, though “firmly”, “with a rugged quality”, “with a firm core to the sound”, or “with robust strength” may also be suitable.
Depending on the musical context, it may imply:
● an angular attack or articulation
● clearly defined accents
● a firm, projecting core to the sound
● a heroic, rugged, or earthy character.
These implications do not apply to every occurrence. In Bruckner, too, a brass-chorale context may call for a weighty, forceful character without emphasizing angularity or roughness.

Italian:
suono della natura

【General meanings】
① A sound of nature (birdsong, wind, a murmuring stream, etc.).
② An inarticulate cry or instinctive vocal sound.

GM uses the term in SYMPHONIE I and SYMPHONIE III. It means “a sound of nature (the resonance of the natural world)”. In SYMPHONIE I, “Wie ein Naturlaut” (translated here as “like a sound of nature”) can be understood as going beyond mere “nature painting”, with a strong suggestion of “something other than an artificially ordered musical tone”. It may be interpreted as a sound originating outside the music (in nature), as though it had already been sounding before the music began: a resonance suggestive of “ambient sound”. In SYMPHONIE III, when the direction for the oboe is combined with “hinaufziehen”, translated as “upward portamento”, the intended effect is probably a mingling of uncontrived natural sound rather than “ambient sound”.

【General meanings】

【Usage notes】
Besides referring to strings themselves, the word occurs in expressions concerning string names, tuning, the use of open strings, and double-stop technique.

A-Saite: Specifies which string to use.
die 'E Saite' auf D herab zu stimmen: An instruction concerning double-bass tuning.
immer auf doppelten Saiten.: A playing instruction for string instruments.
nach den Saiten der Harfe sucht: Here the word refers to the harp strings themselves.
C-Saite nach B herabstimmen: The German note name B denotes B-flat.
keine leeren Saiten benützen!: An instruction intended to allow ample vibrato.

[(Reference score: RS, Tod und Verklärung Op.24, Dover-style reprint: printed p. 151 / PDF p. 49.)](https://el-atril.com/partituras/StraussR/Tod%20und%20Verkl%C3%A4rung/Tod_und_Verkl__rung%20-%20fs.pdf#page=49)

Italian:

Synonymous with Schallbecher when referring to the bell of a wind instrument.

【General meanings】
① The bell of a wind instrument.
② A conical part that amplifies sound; a megaphone.

“Schall” means “sound” or “resonance”.
“Bells up” can be expressed in several ways, including mit aufgehobenem Schalltrichter, Schalltr. auf, and Schalltrichter in die Höhe. Here, “aufgehoben” means “raised”, and “in die Höhe” means “upward” or “up high”.
The bell is also called Schallbecher. No occurrence of Schallbecher has been found in the GM material under investigation, although the word does occur in other score material. In the [RW: Oper] material examined here, Schalltrichter occurs only in Tristan und Isolde WWV 90.

Italian:
acuto, tagliente, severo

【General meanings】
① (Of a blade, etc.) sharp; cutting well.
② (Of taste or smell) pungent; biting; intense.
③ (Of sound, light, the senses, etc.) sharp; severe; harsh.
④ (Of a bend, etc.) sharp.

【Examples in musical contexts】
[GM]
German: Scharf abreissen!
English: Cut off the sound sharply!

[RW: Oper]
German: Colonna mißt Adriano mit scharfem Blick.
English: Colonna sizes Adriano up with a sharp gaze.

[RS: Oper]
German: der jetzt zwischen den beiden andern und der Tür links steht, sehr scharf
English: Now standing between the other two and the door on the left, very sharply.

【Usage notes】
“Sharply”; “clearly”; “acerbically”; “with marked definition (in staccato, etc.)”.

raschiando, strisciando

Italian:
ombra

luce, apparenza, certificato, scontrino, banconota

birichino, malizioso

German: Allmählich verbleicht auch dieses Bild. Der Duft verzieht sich endlich ganz, und zeigt die ganze Grotte einsam und still. Die Grazien verneigen sich schelmisch vor Venus und entfernen sich langsam nach der Liebesgrotte. Tiefste Ruhe. Unveränderte Gruppe der Venus und Tannhäusers.

Italian:
sgabello

Italian:

Italian:
trascinare

【General meanings】
① To drag, pull, or haul (something heavy).
② To trail along the ground (of clothing, etc.).
③ To drag on (of time, etc.).

【Examples in musical contexts】
[GM]
German: Noch einmal so langsam (Nicht schleppend) (𝅘𝅥 = wie zuletzt die 𝅗𝅥)

English: From here on, do not let the tempo drag.

【Usage notes】
“drag (the tempo)”, “slow down”, “let the rhythm become sluggish”, “do not drag the tempo (for nicht schleppen)”.

In GM, “Schleppend” is rendered as “Dragging.”, “nicht schleppend” as “without dragging”, and “Nicht schleppen” as “Do not drag.” Depending on context, “sluggishly” may suit schleppend, while “without becoming sluggish”, “without slowing down”, or “without letting the music drag out” may suit the negative forms.

Schwan means “swan”, and Dreher means “a person who turns something”. Here, the word has been translated as “a person who turns a swan on a spit to roast it”. There are, however, several interpretations of what this word refers to in the folk-song lyrics.

In his 1938 concert notes, Hindemith is said to have explained that this folk song apparently mocked a person who turned a swan on a spit in the kitchen. The translation above follows this interpretation. Another theory holds that the word refers to a player of a hand-cranked organ decorated with a swan.

The title of Hindemith's viola concerto “Der Schwanendreher” comes from the folk song “Seid ihr nicht der Schwanendreher”, which provides the theme for the third movement. In the preface, the composer depicts a travelling musician joining a gathering of people and performing songs and dances brought back from his travels. This is the conception behind the work; it does not establish that the word Schwanendreher itself means “a travelling musician”.

【References】
Journal of the American Viola Society: discussion of the title and the original song (printed pp. 44–46) / Schott: commentary on the work and presentation of the preface

【General meanings】
① A speaking tube (used aboard ships, etc.).
② A spokesperson, publicity representative, or means of communication (for opinions or ideas).
③ A megaphone; a speaking trumpet.

The word is translated as “speaking tube” and, depending on the context, can refer to either:
● a handheld “megaphone” (speaking trumpet) into which one shouts;
● a “speaking tube” aboard a ship or elsewhere (a tube carrying speech from the bridge to the engine room).
The shape and material vary according to the device.

Wagner gives directions for its use in Der fliegende Holländer WWV 63, Die Walküre WWV 86B, and Siegfried WWV 86C; RS does so in Die ägyptische Helena Op.75. In these works, it is specified as a prop or stage acoustic device, affecting the direction in which the voice is projected or the way it sounds.

★ Historical use (nineteenth to early twentieth century)
These directions can be understood as relating to live acoustic effects in which the direction and resonance of the voice are adjusted by passing it through a tube or speaking trumpet. Details of the device’s material, construction, and installation need to be considered in light of documentation for each work and production.
● In Der fliegende Holländer WWV 63, the Steuermann is directed to put the Sprachrohr quickly to his mouth and call out over the side of the ship. Elsewhere in the same work, there is also a direction to call out with both hands held to the mouth.
● In Die Walküre WWV 86B, voices from the background, including Helmwige’s, are directed to be heard through a Sprachrohr.
● For Fafner in Siegfried WWV 86C, Wagner himself gives the direction “durch ein starkes Sprachrohr” (“through a powerful speaking trumpet”). In a later scene, there is also a direction to sing from an opening in the stage floor through a Sprachrohr led to the monster’s mouth from inside. These directions specify the device or route through which the voice passes; specific changes in pitch or timbre need to be considered in light of production documentation and other relevant materials.
● In Die ägyptische Helena Op.75, the Muschel (the omniscient shell) has the direction “d. Sprachrohr”.
These can be understood as stage acoustic techniques for making use of vocal projection, a sense of distance, and timbre.

★ Modern use
The following are possible ways of realising these effects in modern performances. Specific examples of their use, the choice of device, and the positioning of singers and equipment depend on the documentation for individual productions.
● Historical reconstruction (acoustic)
Using an actual speaking trumpet or tube to produce live acoustic effects.
● Electronic processing (microphones and loudspeakers)
Reproducing a voice picked up by a microphone through a loudspeaker to create a sense of distance or reverberation.
● A hybrid approach prioritising visual staging
Combining a prop megaphone with electronic processing to achieve both visual staging and acoustic effects.

Italian:
tono, suono, nota

【General meanings】
① A sound, tone colour or tone.
② A tone of voice, manner of speaking or attitude.
③ A musical note or pitch.

GM frequently uses a family of directions centred on Ton, including “Ton!”, “mit Ton!”, “viel Ton!”, “großer Ton!” and “offener Ton”. Depending on the context, these are rendered as “with a rich tone”, “Make the tone resonate”, and so on. For GM, Ton seems to carry musical nuances extending beyond sheer volume. German Ton is inherently polysemous, covering:
● pitch (how high or low a note is), and a unit of interval in expressions such as ein ganzer Ton;
● sound itself as a physical phenomenon;
● tone colour or resonance, close to Klang;
● expression or manner of speaking (Redeweise, Sprechton);
● artistic tone or atmosphere (emotional tone).
In late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century musical usage, Ton often seems to imply “sonority” or “tone quality”; particularly in Schumann, RW, Brahms, Bruckner and GM, it may be interpreted as referring to the “character”, “density” or “spiritual resonance” of a sound.

1. Ton in vocal music
In “Den Ruf der Schildwachen nachahmen offner Ton!” from “Der Schildwache Nachtlied” in Des Knaben Wunderhorn, offener Ton can be understood as asking for more than simply projecting the voice. It can be understood as recreating the situation of a sentry's call sounding through the darkness, or a piercing call of vigilance. It is rendered as “with an open, resonant voice”.

2. grosser Ton in wind playing
The marking “großer Ton!” for the tenor horn at the beginning of the first movement of SYMPHONIE VII seems to ask for more than playing f or producing a forceful sound: it suggests the sound's “weight”, “presence” and “texture”. In this sense, grosser Ton probably does not refer to volume alone.

3. Ton! in string playing
GM has numerous passages marked simply “Ton!”, especially conspicuous in legato string passages. Here Ton comes close to calling the performer's attention to the sound. One might infer that what GM wanted to avoid was technically accurate but expressionless playing, or treating a melody merely as a structure.

4. viel Ton
“Viel Ton!” in the fourth movement of SYMPHONIE V may often be misunderstood as “many notes” or simply “increase the volume”. It probably asks instead for “density”, “body” or “fullness” of sound: a fully developed resonance.

Abbreviation for Trenner-Verzeichnis.
A number in Franz Trenner’s chronological catalogue of Richard Strauss’s works (Richard Strauss: Werkverzeichnis, 1985; 1993; second revised edition, 1999). TrV and AV are both widely used as reference numbers in research, identification, and the organization of scores.

The difference between TrV and AV
Richard Strauss’s works bear opus numbers assigned during his lifetime (1864–1949), but many early and late works, studies, occasional pieces, and songs have no opus number. Later scholars therefore compiled catalogues to organize and identify the complete body of work systematically. The best-known are AV (Asow numbers) and TrV (Trenner numbers).

Their respective characteristics and functions are as follows.
AV also arranges works chronologically within groups separated by opus-number status and other categories; TrV places compositions in chronological order across those divisions.

1. AV (Asow-Verzeichnis / Müller von Asow numbers)
Compiler: Erich Hermann Müller von Asow
Full title: Richard Strauss: Thematisches Verzeichnis (three volumes, published 1955–1974)
Characteristics and function:
The first large-scale, comprehensive thematic catalogue of Richard Strauss’s works compiled after his death, including musical incipits.
It serves as a scholarly reference and source collection, providing detailed information on opening themes, instrumentation, genesis, autograph locations, first performances and performers, and early printed editions. Müller von Asow died while the third volume was being prepared; Alfons Ott and Franz Trenner completed it. Some later discoveries and information on late works consequently received supplementary treatment.

2. TrV (Trenner-Verzeichnis / Trenner numbers)
Compiler: Franz Trenner
Full title: Richard Strauss: Werkverzeichnis (1985; 1993 edition; second revised edition, 1999, revised by Florian Trenner)
Characteristics and function:
Building on earlier research, this catalogue arranges the works broadly in order of composition, including early works and fragments. Its chronological arrangement surveys Strauss’s output from his early to his late years, making it useful for tracing his creative development and identifying the dates of works. TrV is also used to identify works in Richard Strauss Werke. Kritische Ausgabe and has been adopted as a standard work-number system in library cataloguing.

Examples:
Sonatine No. 1 → TrV 288
Metamorphosen → TrV 290
Oboe Concerto → TrV 292

In summary:
AV: a comprehensive thematic catalogue for investigating incipits, detailed historical and bibliographical information, and the circumstances of composition.
TrV: a chronological catalogue of works, drawing on earlier research to arrange and identify works broadly in chronological order.

These different origins, an earlier detailed thematic catalogue (AV) and a later catalogue that reflects subsequent research and reorganizes the works broadly chronologically (TrV), explain why both sets of numbers are often given in score commentaries and scholarly literature.

Italian:
davanti a sé, tra sé

【General meanings】
① In front of oneself, ahead of oneself; (of what lies ahead) in the future.
② (In a speaking context) to oneself, as if talking to oneself. Whether speech is audible, and how loud it is, depend on the accompanying verb and context.

【Examples in musical contexts】
[RW: Oper]
German: Isolde sich weiter erhebend, sieht Tristan vor sich.
English: Isolde rises further and sees Tristan before her.

[RS: Oper]
German: Er zündet sich eine Pfeife an und bläst behaglich den Rauch vor sich hin
English: He lights a pipe and contentedly puffs away.

【Usage notes】
Literally, “in front of oneself.”
An action may be expressed “outwardly” (including self-directed speech or a low voice), but the phrase need not involve speaking: it can also describe silent reflection or looking ahead.
Possible translations include “as if talking to oneself” and “to oneself (aloud),” according to the context.
By contrast, “für sich” literally means “for oneself.”
It does not invariably mean that the action is “confined inwardly”: it can indicate doing something alone or for oneself, and does not necessarily rule out audible speech.
Possible translations include “inwardly,” “alone” and “privately,” according to the context.

Both are often given Japanese translations meaning “as if talking to oneself.” The presence of audible speech should be decided from the accompanying verb and stage context.

【References】
[LEO, Dr. Bopp: The use of vor sich hin](https://blog.leo.org/2019/07/17/wird-vor-sich-hingesummt-oder-vor-sich-hin-gesummt/)
[Duden: für (für sich)](https://www.duden.de/rechtschreibung/fuer_statt)

“Sound out prominently (above the other parts),” “bring the sound to the foreground.”

I personally suspect that the word in this passage might be a misprint for "verklingend" (gradually becoming softer and dying away). However, some editions print "vorklingend" alongside the Italian instruction "fa risaltare il suono" (make the sound stand out), a literal translation of it, which causes confusion. The International Gustav Mahler Society’s document N_FG_14.pdf shows a copy of the 1967 Weinberger edition bearing corrections entered by Karl Heinz Füssl and Zoltan Roman. On the relevant page, the vowel in "vorklingend" is corrected in red, and "fa risaltare il suono" below it is crossed out.

(= Werke ohne Opuszahl) Works without an opus number (Op.)

In the catalogue of Ludwig van Beethoven’s works by Georg Kinsky and Hans Halm, published in 1955 as Das Werk Beethovens: Thematisch-bibliographisches Verzeichnis seiner sämtlichen vollendeten Kompositionen, commonly known as the Kinsky–Halm catalogue, works without opus numbers were catalogued separately from those with opus numbers under “WoO (Werke ohne Opuszahl)”, and numbered from WoO 1 to WoO 205. These include early works, short pieces, songs, dances, occasional works and arrangements; the designation does not necessarily mean only unpublished works or works discovered posthumously. A well-known example is the Bagatelle in A minor, Für Elise, WoO 59. Further WoO numbers were added on the basis of new research in the revised catalogue published in 2014.

WoO is an abbreviation of the German “Werke ohne Opuszahl”, meaning “works without an opus number”; it is not a designation unique to Ludwig van Beethoven. It is used in catalogues of several composers to classify works without opus numbers, but the numbering systems are independent for each composer and catalogue.

For Johannes Brahms, WoO numbers are assigned to works without opus numbers, arrangements, cadenzas and similar pieces in Johannes Brahms: Thematisch-Bibliographisches Werkverzeichnis, edited by Margit L. McCorkle (1984). For example, the Ungarische Tänze are WoO 1.

For Robert Schumann, WoO numbers were also used in the earlier catalogue by Kurt Hofmann and Siegmar Keil. However, the principal modern scholarly catalogue, Robert Schumann: Thematisch-Bibliographisches Werkverzeichnis, edited by Margit L. McCorkle and commonly known as the Robert-Schumann-Werkverzeichnis (RSW, 2003), assigns WoO 1–8 to works without opus numbers that Schumann published or prepared for publication, while other fragments, unpublished works, projects and similar materials are classified chiefly in the Anhang (appendix).

WoO numbers are also sometimes used for certain works by Felix Mendelssohn Bartholdy in older scores and recording documentation. However, the current standard catalogue, the Mendelssohn-Werkverzeichnis (MWV, 2009), uses its own genre-based numbering system, such as MWV U 136, rather than WoO as its principal formal classification.

Thus, WoO is a classification used for several composers, but it is not a single, unified system of work numbers shared by musicology as a whole. In general contexts, “WoO 59” without a composer’s name often refers to Ludwig van Beethoven’s Für Elise, but in precise writing it is advisable to include the composer’s name.

See also “Hess”.

Italian:

【General meanings】
① (As a preposition) To, at, in.
② (As an adverb) Too; excessively.
③ (As an adverb) Shut; closed.

【Examples in musical contexts】
“In a particular state,” “too,” “to (in relation to).”

In musical directions, the function of zu varies considerably depending on the words that follow it.

1. Indicating degree (too / troppo)
Placed before an adjective, it means “too,” with a negative connotation of excess.
“Nicht zu schnell”: not too fast (similar in sense to Non troppo allegro).
“Nicht zu mäßig”: not too moderate or restrained.

2. Specifying the number of players or instruments
“zu 2 (zu zwei)”: with two instruments, or with two players (whether they play in unison depends on the score). (Equivalent to the Italian a 2.)
“zu 3 (zu drei)”: with three instruments.

3. Specifying a state or manner
“zu Ende”: at an end, finished; (in expressions such as “zu Ende spielen”) (playing) through to the end.
“Mund zu”: with the mouth closed (as in humming).

4. Directions for a particular playing technique
“Dämpfer zu”: interpreted here as meaning to put on the mute (sense ③). Incidentally, “Dämpfer auf” in GM also means to put on the mute. See the entry “Dämpfer auf.”
